extracted.intended_audience: academic librarians, library staff, and administrators responsible for supporting distance and online learners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and best practices for designing, staffing, and delivering library services (technical access, reference, instruction, partnerships) tailored to distance and online learners. Emphasis on information literacy, virtual reference modalities, e-reserves, and institutional collaboration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploration and use of social tagging to enhance discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: Libraries should explore the possibilities created by social tagging (allowing librarians and patrons to tag resources found in library catalogues, including e-resources).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: vendor products (e.g., Innovative Interfaces’ Encore) that permit user tagging. Social tagging can augment the library's Web presence and resource discovery capabilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implement electronic course reserves (e-reserves)
rubrics_metrics.description: Replace or supplement traditional physical course reserves with e-reserves to provide selected course items via the Web for students in particular courses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Benefits: avoids limited physical copies/short loans, supports a variety of digital formats (video, audio, simulations), and aligns with diverse learning objectives and styles. Challenges include time-consuming scanning/mounting and securing copyright permissions; many libraries use commercial systems or develop in-house solutions (examples: SDSU Docutek ERes, Athabasca University’s Digital Reading Room).

rubrics_metrics.name: Optimize licensed content access via persistent linking and proxy authentication
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide direct, persistent links to subscribed database content and manage licensed content access through proxy servers to permit only authorized users.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Licensed contents (e.g., journal articles) require authentication; non-licensed web resources can be public. Search across course collections supports multidisciplinary access. Design systems to encourage inclusion of diverse digital formats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide robust technical support for remote access and authentication
rubrics_metrics.description: Address login/password issues, browser configuration, software installation, and other troubleshooting for virtual library users promptly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure front-line library staff training, clear website instructions, coordination with computing services, and multiple contact methods (email, web forms, toll-free telephone) to reduce frustrating access problems for e-learners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offer meaningful reference services beyond mere access
rubrics_metrics.description: E-learners require more than access to resources; reference librarians should provide expertise to help make sense of systems, research tools, and the research process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reference support must adapt to remote contexts; it should include interpretive help and guidance, not just pointing to resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use email reference judiciously and understand its trade-offs
rubrics_metrics.description: Email has been the most common means for electronic reference, offering global/time-independent access and a written record, but lacks verbal and non-verbal cues of face-to-face interviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advantages: written record, time to reflect, electronic transmission of results. Disadvantages: potential loss of nuance and diagnostic cues; may impact the quality of reference interviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design web reference forms to elicit complete request information
rubrics_metrics.description: Well-designed reference web forms should encourage e-learners to include full identifying and course information, a clear description of the research problem, search terminology, and assignment parameters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good forms reduce ambiguity and follow-up. Use automated acknowledgements to reassure users and set expectations for service response times (example: Athabasca University ‘Ask about a Research Topic’ page).

rubrics_metrics.name: Complement email with real-time communication tools where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Enhance interaction via chat/instant messaging to provide more immediate two-way text-based communication between librarians and e-learners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose programs appropriate to institutional needs—vendor systems may offer co-browsing, patron queuing, file sharing, and richer statistics; instant messaging is widely familiar but some require downloads and may discourage use. Consider multi-account clients (e.g., Trillian, Pidgin) to consolidate platforms and reduce monitoring overhead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Participate in virtual reference consortia to extend coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Virtual reference consortia enable libraries to answer questions from e-learners in other parts of the consortium service area, expanding time-zone and hours coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consortia increase immediate availability of librarians, helpful for different time zones. Note limitation: chat may still be insufficient for complex inquiries—follow-up via email or telephone may be necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize limits of chat for complex questions and provide appropriate follow-up
rubrics_metrics.description: While chat can resolve some transactions, complex research help often requires time to develop search strategies and may need follow-up by email or telephone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use chat for straightforward assistance or to schedule deeper help; provide telephone support for intricate inquiries, ideally when both parties can access the Internet concurrently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain telephone reference as an effective strategy for complex inquiries
rubrics_metrics.description: Providing a toll-free telephone number remains an effective reference strategy for intricate inquiries and works best when both librarian and e-learner are working at Internet-connected computers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Telephone interviews allow verbal cues and can be combined with screen-sharing or email follow-up for comprehensive assistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach and promote information literacy per ACRL competency standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt information literacy competencies so students can determine information needs, access information effectively, evaluate sources critically, use information to accomplish purposes, and understand ethical/legal/social issues of information use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ACRL five standards: (1) determine nature/extent of needed information; (2) access effectively/efficiently; (3) evaluate and incorporate critically; (4) use information effectively individually or in groups; (5) understand economic/legal/social issues and use information ethically and legally. Integrate these into instruction and curriculum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promote critical information literacy beyond competency checklists
rubrics_metrics.description: Encourage critical reflection about information and knowledge—recognize knowledge as socially constructed and contested—and discuss limitations of peer-review and alternative voices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critical information literacy draws on critical theory and education; e.g., teach the value of peer-reviewed journals while also examining how alternative voices may be silenced and how to find alternative literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design online tutorials and courses that foster information literacy and active learning
rubrics_metrics.description: Create interactive tutorials and online courses (from brief orientation to in-depth research process instruction) that promote active learning and information literacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: TILT (Texas Information Literacy Tutorial), Internet Navigator, SAFARI, MOSAIC, and full courses like Athabasca’s INFS 200. Use established models and collaborative materials where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide context-specific, point-of-need help and brief multimedia tutorials
rubrics_metrics.description: Place links to tutorials at points of need; use animated tutorials and brief voice-over demonstrations of database features within real search contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tools: ViewletBuilder, Camtasia, Captivate. Brief tutorials with voice-over are particularly effective. Joining collaborative initiatives (e.g., COPPUL ANTS) reduces workload and avoids reinventing materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enhance tutorials with interactive/group instruction and embedded librarian roles
rubrics_metrics.description: Supplement isolated tutorials with interactive instruction (e.g., chat-simulated classrooms) and embed librarians in LMS as TAs, co-instructors, or co-designers to increase awareness and integration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Florida Distance Learning Reference Center experimenting with chat for live group instruction; embedding librarians improves access to expertise within course contexts and supports teaching and learning objectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use podcasting and video for accessible instructional delivery
rubrics_metrics.description: Deliver instructional materials via podcasts and video clips to allow e-learners 'anytime, anywhere' access, matching mobile device usage trends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: libcasts (Mount Allison University) downloadable/subscribable via iTunes. Use media for everything from orientation to in-depth research tutorials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize human components (service tradition and human interaction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that technology is infrastructure but human factors (service tradition, rapport, communication) determine virtual library success; address lack of face-to-face opportunities and awareness of services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop strategies to build rapport remotely, improve communication channels, and raise user awareness of library services to avoid poor communication between staff and e-learners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop librarian–faculty partnerships and liaison roles
rubrics_metrics.description: Foster collaboration with faculty, researchers, and departments through librarian-liaison roles to support resources, services, and instructional support aligned with course needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Liaison librarians focus on communication channels and the effects of technology to share knowledge, contribute to responsive course design, incorporate student feedback, and help integrate information literacy into curricula.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secure senior management support and institutional planning
rubrics_metrics.description: Obtain leadership, funding, and administrative involvement across the institution to support virtual library development and ensure appropriate services and values are understood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Canadian Library Association Guidelines emphasize responsibilities in funding, administration, personnel, facilities, resources, services, publicity, and professional development; advocate advance planning in consultation with faculty and campus personnel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include all staff in partnership and provide ongoing training
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure all staff involved in e-learner support are included in collaborative efforts and receive ongoing training to upgrade skills and adapt to changing roles and technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instill a culture of sharing, motivation, equity, and active partnering to reduce fear of change and enable staff to respond positively to new assignments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage external partnerships and consortia to expand services
rubrics_metrics.description: Use external collaborations (reciprocal borrowing agreements, virtual reference networks, consortia subscriptions) to broaden access to physical and electronic resources and staff expertise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Canadian University Reciprocal Borrowing Agreement, Virtual Reference Canada, LHCADL for shared digital resources; consortia can include information literacy/training components to share expertise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge institutional ethical obligation to provide appropriate library support
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutions that provide distance and online education have an ethical obligation to ensure learners have access to appropriate library support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Library support should be planned and resourced to meet online learners' needs and ensure equity of access to academic resources and services.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design learner supports to be flexible, accessible, and readily available
rubrics_metrics.description: Learner supports should foster independence and be flexible, accessible, and available when needed to promote persistence and reduce dropout.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supports may include academic/tutorial help, technical assistance, reference services, and non-academic supports; the aim is a learner-support system where students feel valued and find services manageable.
